title: An inter-lake level split raised six-month Michigan-Huron interval score by 0.65% at 1990-2024 origins
abstract: We tested whether a large difference between standardized seasonal level anomalies in Superior and Michigan-Huron helps set six-month 90% forecast intervals for Michigan-Huron. Both rules used the same linear point forecast with local history and current Superior level. Each annual calibration used only earlier completed forecast errors. Across 420 monthly origins in 1990-2024, a median split on absolute inter-lake imbalance raised mean interval score by 0.65%. The conditional 95% five-year block interval for the increase was 0.09% to 1.29%. Coverage fell from 92.62% to 92.38%, while mean width rose from 47.87 to 48.10 cm. Three- and ten-year blocks also gave increases. A twenty-year calibration window left the difference uncertain. This is a small negative benchmark for this split rule, not evidence against physical lake coupling or all state-based uncertainty methods. Revised data, overlapping errors, 35 test years, model choice and conditional intervals limit inference. The package includes attributed numerical inputs, source hashes, code, every interval, all score draws, a figure and a numerical audit.

display.caption: Score reductions for all planned split rules and descriptive coverage by imbalance state. Negative reduction means worse intervals. Limits condition on stored forecasts.
